3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual and wise. Paul tells them bluntly that their quarrelling over leaders shows they are still spiritual infants, behaving like ordinary unconverted people. Their leaders are only servants. Using a farming picture, Paul says he planted and Apollos watered, but God made things grow, so the workers are nothing and God is everything. Then a building picture: Paul laid the only possible foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it. On the day of judgement, fire will test the quality of each builder’s work; good work will be rewarded, and poor work will burn up, though the builder himself will be saved, as if escaping through flames.

Then a warning: the church is God’s temple, where his Spirit lives, and anyone who destroys it will be destroyed by God. Paul ends where chapter 1 began, with the folly of the world’s wisdom. No one should boast about human leaders, because everything already belongs to believers, Paul, Apollos, Peter, the world, life, death, the present and the future, and they belong to Christ, and Christ to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul could not speak to them as spiritually mature people, but only as people still ruled by the flesh, infants in Christ. He gave them milk rather than solid food, because they were not ready, and they still are not. Their jealousy and quarrels prove it: they are behaving like ordinary people, saying “I follow Paul” or “I follow Apollos”. But Paul and Apollos are only servants through whom they believed, each doing the job the Lord assigned. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth, so the planter and the waterer are nothing; only God, who makes things grow, matters. The workers have one purpose, and each will be rewarded for his own work. They are God’s fellow workers; the church is God’s field and God’s building.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated insistence that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is the Reformed doctrine of sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Paul preached; Apollos taught; but neither of them converted a single soul. Conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of the preacher. This means that the minister cannot take credit for results, cannot despair over apparent fruitlessness as if it were his own failure, and cannot be compared with another minister as if their different “results” reflected their different competencies. God gives where and when he wills.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions were measuring Paul and Apollos by their outputs — converts, rhetorical impact, visible results. Paul refuses this measuring rod: the results belong to God, not to the apostle. Now: The contemporary church is still tempted to evaluate ministry by attendance, conversion numbers, and cultural impact — and to attribute these to the skill and gifting of the human leader. Paul’s corrective: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God of growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 3 applies chapters 1–2 to the Corinthians’ divisions. First, their quarrelling proves they are still spiritually immature, acting like mere humans, not people of the Spirit (vv. 1–4). Second, Paul and Apollos are only servants. One planted, one watered, but God gave the growth. The church is God’s field and God’s building (vv. 5–9). Third, Paul laid the only foundation, Jesus Christ; everyone who builds on it must take care, for the Day will test each one’s work by fire. Good work will be rewarded; worthless work will burn, though the builder himself is saved (vv. 10–15). Fourth, the church is God’s holy temple, where his Spirit dwells; whoever destroys it, God will destroy (vv. 16–17). Finally, do not boast in human leaders. All things are yours, Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present and future, because you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (vv. 18–23).

But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people. Key words. The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual (pneumatikoi), wise and mature. Paul says: you were not acting like it.

But as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. Key words. “Of the flesh” (sarkinos, made of flesh). Here it describes believers who are still governed too much by the old ways of thinking. “Infants” (nēpioi, babies) in Christ: they are in Christ, truly believers, but immature.

I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. Key words. Milk: the basic truths of the gospel. Solid food: deeper teaching and application (Hebrews 5:12–14). When Paul first came, they were new believers and could only take milk. That was normal.

And even now you are not yet ready. Key words. What is not normal: years later, they still cannot take solid food. They have not grown.

Where Christians differ: the carnal Christian. Some teach that there are two kinds of Christians: spiritual Christians, who have surrendered to Christ as Lord, and carnal Christians, who have accepted Christ as Saviour but live permanently as if unconverted. Verdict: Paul is rebuking immaturity in true believers, not describing a permanent, acceptable category of Christian. The Corinthians were in Christ, and some still behaved in fleshly ways, which Paul calls them to leave behind. All true believers have the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and are being changed (2 Corinthians 3:18), though at different speeds. A profession of faith that never produces any change is not saving faith (James 2:17; 1 John 3:9–10). Christ is received as both Saviour and Lord.

What it does not mean. It does not mean milk is bad, or that the gospel is only for beginners. The gospel is the food at every stage. Solid food is the same gospel, more deeply understood and applied.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul could not address you as people who live by the Spirit but as people who are still worldly, mere infants in Christ. He gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for it. Indeed, you are still not ready.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: am I growing? Are my reactions and attitudes more like Christ than a year ago? If not, ask God for growth, and feed on his word.

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?

For you are still of the flesh. Key words. “Of the flesh” here is sarkikos, fleshly: governed by sinful human nature.

For while there is jealousy and strife among you. Key words. The evidence. Jealousy (zēlos, envy, rivalry) and strife (eris, quarrelling). These are listed among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20).

Are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way? Key words. Literally, walking according to man. They are behaving just like unbelievers, like the competitive culture of Corinth around them. Fan clubs and rivalries are normal in the world; they should not be normal in the church.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sexual sins are fleshly. Paul’s first example of fleshliness is quarrelling and jealousy in church. Respectable sins are still sins of the flesh.

In a sentence. You are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and quarrelling among you, are you not worldly? Are you not acting like mere humans?

For worship. Confess any jealousy or rivalry you feel toward other Christians. Ask the Spirit to replace it with love.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.

For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? Key words. Paul names only himself and Apollos now, perhaps because they were the two who had worked in Corinth, or to avoid naming Peter.

What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Key words. Notice “what,” not “who.” Paul asks what their function is, not their personal importance.

Servants through whom you believed. Key words. “Servants” (diakonoi): household servants, waiters. They were instruments (through whom), not sources (in whom). You believed in Christ, through them.

As the Lord assigned to each. Key words. Each servant was given his task by the Lord. Paul’s gifts and Apollos’s gifts were both from Christ. No reason for rivalry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers deserve no honour. Elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17). But they are servants, not masters.

In a sentence. For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere human beings? What, after all, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Only servants, through whom you came to believe, as the Lord has assigned to each his task.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your pastor, and pray for him. But do not put him on a pedestal. He is a servant, as you are.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.

I planted. Key words. Paul founded the church in Corinth: he first brought the gospel there (Acts 18:1–11).

Apollos watered. Key words. Apollos came later and built up the young church with his teaching (Acts 18:27–19:1).

But God gave the growth. Key words. The tense is different. Planted and watered are past, completed actions. Gave the growth is imperfect: God was continually causing growth. Paul and Apollos did their parts at certain times; God was doing the real work all along.

So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. Key words. Compared to God, the workers are nothing. No gardener makes a seed grow. Only God gives life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean human work is unnecessary. God uses planting and watering. Without them there is no harvest. But the result belongs to God.

In a sentence. Paul planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God has been making it grow. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow.

For worship. If you have seen anyone grow in faith through your efforts, give God the glory. He gave the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.

He who plants and he who waters are one. Key words. One in purpose and work: on the same team, serving the same Lord, aiming at the same harvest. The Corinthians made them rivals; they were partners.

And each will receive his wages according to his labor. Key words. Wages (misthos, reward). Each worker will be rewarded individually by God. Not according to success, which belongs to God, but according to labour (kopos, toil): faithfulness in hard work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by labour. Salvation is a gift (Romans 6:23). Rewards for faithful service are themselves gracious, God crowning his own gifts.

In a sentence. The one who plants and the one who waters have one purpose, and they will each be rewarded according to their own labour.

On a Tuesday. God rewards faithfulness, not visible success. Keep labouring in your quiet corner. He sees.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.

For we are God’s fellow workers. Key words. “God’s” is emphatic in Greek: three times in this verse. Fellow workers (synergoi): probably workers together under God, belonging to God, rather than working alongside God as equals. Paul and Apollos are fellow workers in God’s service.

You are God’s field. Key words. The agricultural picture of verses 6–8. The church belongs to God, not to Paul or Apollos.

God’s building. Key words. Paul switches pictures to prepare for verses 10–17. The church is a building under construction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church belongs to its members or its ministers to run as they please. It is God’s.

In a sentence. For we are co-workers in God’s service; you are God’s field, God’s building.

For worship. Your church is God’s field and God’s building. Pray for its growth, and do your part in it.

parallels.desc: the planting of the LORD

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By God’s grace, Paul laid the foundation like a skilled master builder, and others are building on it. Everyone must be careful how they build, because no other foundation can be laid than the one already there, Jesus Christ. On that foundation people build with gold, silver and precious stones, or with wood, hay and straw. The day of judgement will expose each person’s work, because it will be revealed with fire, which will test its quality. If the work survives, the builder will be rewarded; if it burns up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through fire. Paul then warns that the church is God’s temple, in which God’s Spirit lives. If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person, because God’s temple is holy, and they are that temple.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

Paul’s identification of the church as God’s temple carries enormous theological weight in a letter written to a city famous for its pagan temples. The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the temple of Aphrodite; the city was saturated with temple culture, sexual licence, and temple feasts. Paul’s claim is that the living God has abandoned temples made of stone and taken up residence in a community of people — flawed, fractious, sin-prone people — through his Spirit. The church is not a building where God may be found; the church is the people in whom God actually dwells. This is the new covenant fulfilment of every OT temple theology: God with his people, no longer mediated through architecture and ritual, but through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were not merely social dysfunction; they were a theological emergency. A fragmented community cannot be a temple — the architectural metaphor itself requires unity, all the stones fitting together. The faction wars were, quite literally, demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: Every church split, every faction, every deliberate destruction of community is an assault on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. This gives a theological gravity to church unity that mere social concern cannot supply: we are not trying to be nice; we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

According to the grace of God given to me. Key words. Paul’s apostleship and skill were gifts of grace (15:10).

Like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation. Key words. “Master builder” (architektōn, from which architect): the chief builder who oversees the project. “Skilled” (sophos, wise): the true wisdom, unlike the Corinthians’ worldly wisdom.

And someone else is building upon it. Key words. Apollos, and other teachers since. Every generation of teachers builds on the foundation.

Let each one take care how he builds upon it. Key words. A warning to teachers and leaders: be careful what you build with. The quality of your teaching and ministry matters.

For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Key words. Christ crucified, as preached by the apostles, is the only foundation (Isaiah 28:16; Ephesians 2:20). No one may lay a different one. A church built on any other foundation is not a church of God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Paul himself is the foundation. Christ is. Paul laid it by preaching Christ.

In a sentence. By the grace God has given him, Paul laid a foundation as a wise builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one should build with care. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you build, a family, a ministry, a life, build it on Christ. Nothing else will stand.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw—each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.

Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw. Key words. Two kinds of materials. Gold, silver and precious stones were used in the temple (1 Chronicles 29:2): durable and precious. Wood, hay and straw were used for ordinary huts: cheap and flammable. The materials stand for the quality of a teacher’s work: sound teaching and faithful ministry, or shallow, worldly ministry.

Each one’s work will become manifest. Key words. Now it may be hard to tell the difference. On the Day, it will be obvious.

For the Day will disclose it. Key words. The Day: the day of the Lord, Christ’s return and judgement (1:8; 4:5).

Because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. Key words. Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up. Fire here is a picture of God’s searching judgement (Malachi 3:2–3; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). It tests the work, not the person’s salvation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only full-time ministers will be judged. Paul speaks first of teachers in the church, but the principle applies to every believer’s service.

In a sentence. If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, their work will be shown for what it is, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work.

For worship. Ask God to help you build with gold: faithful truth, sincere love, work done for his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up.

parallels.desc: like a refiner’s fire

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.

If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. Key words. Faithful work will stand the test and be rewarded (Matthew 25:21).

If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss. Key words. Loss of reward: the work is gone, as if a lifetime’s labour went up in smoke.

Though he himself will be saved. Key words. The builder is a true believer, built on Christ. His salvation does not depend on the quality of his work but on the foundation.

But only as through fire. Key words. Like a man escaping a burning house with nothing but his life. Saved, but with nothing to show.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. The Roman Catholic Church has used this passage to support purgatory, a place of temporal purifying punishment after death for believers before entering heaven. Verdict: The passage does not teach purgatory. The fire tests works, not people; it happens on the Day of judgement, not over a period after death; and it is about the work of teachers, not punishment for sins. Christ’s sacrifice fully paid for his people’s sins, so there is no punishment left for them (Hebrews 10:14; Romans 8:1). At death, believers go immediately to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Westminster 32.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faithfulness does not matter, since we are saved anyway. Loss of reward is real loss, and there is shame in it (1 John 2:28).

In a sentence. If what has been built survives, the builder will receive a reward. If it is burned up, the builder will suffer loss but yet will be saved, even though only as one escaping through the flames.

On a Tuesday. Will what you are doing today survive the fire? Invest in what lasts: people, truth, love.

parallels.desc: a brand plucked out of the burning

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

Do you not know that you are God’s temple. Key words. “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple. Temple here is naos, the inner sanctuary where God dwelt, not the whole temple complex. Paul says the local church is God’s holy of holies. In 6:19 he will say each believer’s body is a temple.

And that God’s Spirit dwells in you? Key words. As the glory-cloud filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11), so God’s Spirit lives among his gathered people. The church is where God is.

If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. Key words. The same verb twice (phtheirō, ruin, corrupt, destroy). Whoever wrecks the church, by divisive factions, false teaching or corrupting influence, God will ruin. This is not a builder who builds badly (vv. 12–15), but a wrecker. God guards his temple fiercely.

For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. Key words. Holy: set apart for God. Damaging the church is an attack on what belongs to God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer who causes trouble will lose salvation. It describes those who destroy the church, showing they were never truly of it, and warns all of us how seriously God takes the unity and purity of his church.

In a sentence. Don’t you know that you yourselves are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in your midst? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person; for God’s temple is sacred, and you together are that temple.

For worship. When your church gathers, God is present by his Spirit. Come with reverence, and guard its unity.
verseByVerse.note: “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to fool themselves. Anyone who thinks he is wise by this world’s standards should become a fool, in the world’s eyes, so as to become truly wise. The world’s wisdom is foolishness to God, as Scripture says: God traps the wise in their cunning, and knows how empty their reasoning is. So no one should boast about human leaders. Everything already belongs to them: Paul, Apollos and Peter, the world, life and death, the present and the future. All of it is theirs, and they belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great catalogue texts of what it means to be in Christ. Paul’s list — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present, future — is comprehensive: every apostle, every circumstance, every temporal horizon, even death itself, belongs to the believer in Christ. The Corinthians have been acting poor — squabbling over which apostle to claim — while they are infinitely rich. This is union with Christ expanded to cosmic scope: the one who is in Christ owns, in principle, everything that Christ owns. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and infinitely more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming one-third of the apostolic inheritance — “I follow Paul,” etc. — when they could have had the whole. Their factionalism was a self-imposed poverty in the middle of infinite wealth. Now: The Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing — claiming a slice when the whole belongs to him. The traditions are real and valuable; they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”

Let no one deceive himself. Key words. Self-deception is the danger of the clever. They think they are wise, and so cannot see their folly.

If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. Key words. To become wise, you must accept being thought a fool by the world, by embracing the foolish message of the cross (1:18–25).

For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. Key words. In God’s eyes, the world’s wisdom, apart from him, is foolishness.

For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness.” Key words. From Job 5:13, the only quotation of Job in the New Testament outside Romans 11. God traps the clever in their own schemes. Their cleverness becomes their snare.

And again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.” Key words. From Psalm 94:11. Futile (mataios, empty, vain). God sees through all human reasoning that leaves him out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. It means that wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10), and all learning must bow to God’s revelation.

In a sentence. Do not deceive yourselves. If any of you think you are wise by the standards of this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness”; and again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”

On a Tuesday. Be willing to look foolish in the world’s eyes for believing God’s word. That is the beginning of real wisdom.

parallels.desc: he catches the wise in their own craftiness
the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,

So let no one boast in men. Key words. The conclusion of chapters 1–3. Do not boast in human leaders. The party slogans must stop.

For all things are yours. Key words. A glorious reversal. You said, I belong to Paul. Paul says: no, Paul belongs to you. Why pick one teacher when God has given you all of them?

Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas. Key words. All the teachers are God’s gifts to you, to serve you (Ephesians 4:11–12).

Or the world. Key words. The whole created world is yours, as heirs with Christ (Romans 4:13; 8:17; Matthew 5:5).

Or life or death. Key words. Life serves you, and death serves you, for it brings you to Christ (Philippians 1:21). Death is no longer your master; it is your servant.

Or the present or the future—all are yours. Key words. Present circumstances and future events: all work together for your good (Romans 8:28, 38).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians own everything now or can grasp at things. It means that in Christ, everything is working for them, and they will inherit it all.

In a sentence. So then, no more boasting about human leaders! All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future, all are yours,

For worship. Life is yours. Death is yours. The future is yours. Praise God for such riches in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

And you are Christ’s. Key words. All things belong to you, because you belong to Christ. Not to Paul, not to Apollos, but to Christ. This is the true slogan: I am Christ’s. And the reason all things are yours is that they are his, and you are in him.

And Christ is God’s. Key words. Christ, as the Son and Mediator, belongs to God the Father and serves his glory (11:3; 15:28). Everything flows down from God, through Christ, to his people, and everything flows back up to God’s glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is less than God in his divine nature. As the eternal Son, he is equal with the Father. As Mediator, the Son incarnate, he willingly serves the Father’s purpose (John 14:28; Philippians 2:6–11).

In a sentence. and you are of Christ, and Christ is of God.

On a Tuesday. You belong to Christ. When someone tries to claim your loyalty, whether a leader, a cause, a party, remember whose you are.

4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Paul finishes his answer to the factions by telling the Corinthians how to think about their leaders. Apostles are Christ’s servants and the managers of God’s revealed truth, and what counts for a manager is faithfulness. Paul is not troubled by the Corinthians’ assessment of him, or even by his own clear conscience, because the Lord is his judge, and on the last day he will expose hidden motives and give each person whatever praise is due. So the Corinthians must stop judging prematurely and stop puffing themselves up over one teacher against another, for everything they have is a gift.

Then Paul turns to biting irony. The Corinthians act as if they have already arrived, rich and reigning like kings, while the apostles look like condemned prisoners paraded at the end of a procession: hungry, ill-clothed, beaten, homeless, labouring with their hands, treated as the scum of the earth, yet blessing those who curse them. He writes not to shame them but to warn them as a father. They may have countless tutors, but only one father in the gospel, so they should imitate him. He is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways, and will come himself soon to see whether the arrogant have any real power, since God’s kingdom is a matter of power, not talk. Should he come with a rod, or with love and gentleness?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People should regard Paul and his fellow workers as Christ’s servants, entrusted with managing God’s revealed secrets, and the one thing required of such managers is that they prove faithful. Paul cares very little whether the Corinthians or any human court evaluates him; he does not even judge himself. His conscience is clear, but that does not prove him innocent; the Lord is the one who judges him. So they should not pass verdicts before the time. When the Lord comes he will bring hidden things to light and reveal the purposes of every heart, and then each person will receive whatever commendation comes from God. Paul has used himself and Apollos as an example so that they learn not to go beyond what Scripture says and not to be proud of one leader against another. What makes anyone superior? What do they have that they did not receive? And if it was a gift, why boast as if it were not?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatological Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pre-judge himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism but eschatological realism. The final judgment has not yet been rendered; therefore all present judgments — including self-assessment — are provisional. Reformed theology has always warned against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned): both pre-empt the judgment that belongs to God alone. The practical implication is freedom: neither to be destroyed by human criticism nor to be puffed up by human praise, because neither the critic nor the flatterer is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were evaluating Paul and finding him wanting, not by the standard of faithfulness but by the standards of rhetorical eloquence and visible success. Paul refuses the evaluation: you are not my judge; the Lord is. Now: Ministry evaluation by attendance, public approval, or conference invitations is the contemporary equivalent. The minister who structures his ministry around what will get him praised by his peers has already chosen the wrong judge. The only evaluation that matters is the Lord’s — and it will assess what the heart actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 4 finishes Paul’s answer to the divisions of chapters 1–4. First, ministers are servants and stewards; what matters is faithfulness, and only the Lord can judge it, at his coming. So the Corinthians must stop ranking their teachers (vv. 1–5). Second, everything they have was received as a gift, so they have no ground for pride (vv. 6–7). Third, with biting irony, Paul contrasts their self-satisfied sense of already reigning with the apostles’ real life: hungry, beaten, homeless, treated as the scum of the world (vv. 8–13). Finally, Paul speaks as their spiritual father. He warns them as beloved children, sends Timothy, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or with gentle love (vv. 14–21). The cross shapes not only the message but the messenger’s life.

This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ. Key words. “Servants” here is hypēretai, a word used of assistants, attendants, originally under-rowers on a ship. Ministers are Christ’s assistants, under his orders.

And stewards of the mysteries of God. Key words. A steward (oikonomos) was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods and servants (Luke 12:42). The mysteries of God are the truths once hidden and now revealed in the gospel (2:7). Ministers do not own the message; they manage it on God’s behalf, handing it out faithfully to the household.

Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Key words. The one requirement is faithfulness (pistos): trustworthy, reliable, loyal to the master. Not eloquence, popularity or success.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are a priestly class who dispense grace through rituals. The mysteries are the gospel truths, which they proclaim. They are stewards of a message.

In a sentence. This, then, is how you ought to regard us: as servants of Christ and as those entrusted with the mysteries God has revealed. Now it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful.

On a Tuesday. Whatever God has entrusted to you, your family, your job, your gifts, the one question is: am I faithful with it?
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.

But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. Key words. The Corinthians were evaluating their teachers, comparing Paul unfavourably with others. “Judged” (anakrinō, examined, cross-examined, as in a preliminary hearing). Literally by any human day: a human day of judgement, as opposed to the Lord’s Day. Paul does not care much about their verdict.

In fact, I do not even judge myself. Key words. Paul does not even trust his own assessment of himself.

For I am not aware of anything against myself. Key words. His conscience is clear about his ministry among them. He knows of no unfaithfulness.

But I am not thereby acquitted. Key words. “Acquitted” (dikaioō, justified, declared righteous). A clear conscience is not the final verdict. Conscience can be wrong or blind. Paul is not saying his salvation is uncertain, but that his faithfulness as a servant will be assessed by the Lord, not by his own feelings.

It is the Lord who judges me. Key words. Christ alone is qualified to evaluate his servants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are above accountability or criticism. Elders can be rebuked for sin (1 Timothy 5:19–20). It means the final evaluation of a servant’s faithfulness belongs to Christ, and ministers should not live for human approval.

In a sentence. Paul cares very little if he is judged by you or by any human court; indeed, he does not even judge himself. His conscience is clear, but that does not make him innocent. It is the Lord who judges him.

For worship. Ask the Lord to search your heart (Psalm 139:23–24). Then rest in his judgement, not in others’ opinions or even your own.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.

Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time. Key words. The Corinthians were acting as judges of their ministers before the real judgement day. Stop ranking and rating.

Before the Lord comes. Key words. The time of judgement is the return of Christ.

Who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness. Key words. Not necessarily evil things, but everything hidden from human view.

And will disclose the purposes of the heart. Key words. “Purposes” (boulai, counsels, motives). Only God sees motives. Two ministers may do the same thing, one for Christ’s glory, one for his own. Only the Lord knows which.

Then each one will receive his commendation from God. Key words. “Commendation” (epainos, praise). A surprisingly positive conclusion: the Lord will find something to praise in each faithful servant. It is from God that praise matters (Romans 2:29).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may never make any judgements now. In the next chapter, Paul commands the church to judge a sinning member (5:12). What is forbidden is judging motives and ranking servants of Christ as if we could see their hearts.

In a sentence. Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of the heart. At that time each will receive their praise from God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot see other people’s motives. Give them the benefit of the doubt, and leave the heart to God.

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?

I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers. Key words. “Applied” (metaschēmatizō, changed the form of). Paul used himself and Apollos as examples, so that he would not have to name the leaders the Corinthians were actually quarrelling over.

That you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written. Key words. Probably a known saying. What is written is Scripture, which Paul has quoted repeatedly in chapters 1–3 (1:19, 31; 2:9, 16; 3:19–20). Stay within the limits of Scripture. Do not judge ministers by worldly standards that Scripture does not give.

That none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. Key words. “Puffed up” (physioō, inflated like a pair of bellows). A key word in this letter (4:18–19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4). Pride was their great problem.

For who sees anything different in you? Key words. Who makes you superior? Who says you are better than others?

What do you have that you did not receive? Key words. One of the great humbling questions of the Bible. Your life, your gifts, your faith, your knowledge, your salvation: all received as gifts.

If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? Key words. Boasting in a gift is absurd. You boast in the giver.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Some churches hold that tradition or church authority has equal standing with Scripture, adding doctrines Scripture does not teach. Verdict: Not going beyond what is written expresses the principle the Reformers called sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority for faith and life. Teachers and traditions are useful servants, but nothing may be required of Christians as necessary that is not taught in Scripture or drawn from it by good and necessary consequence (Westminster 1.6, 1.10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may never use books or creeds. These are helpful as long as they serve and agree with Scripture.

In a sentence. Now, brothers and sisters, Paul has applied these things to himself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us the meaning of the saying, “Do not go beyond what is written.” Then you will not be puffed up in being a follower of one of us over against the other. For who makes you different from anyone else? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?

For worship. List three things you are proud of. Then thank God for each, as gifts you received.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to irony. The Corinthians act as if they already have everything, already rich and reigning as kings without the apostles. He wishes they really did reign, so that the apostles could share it. Instead God seems to have put the apostles at the end of the procession, like men condemned to die in the arena, a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people. The apostles are fools for Christ, weak and dishonoured, while the Corinthians think themselves wise, strong and honoured. To this very hour the apostles are hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten and homeless; they work hard with their own hands; when cursed they bless, when persecuted they endure, when slandered they answer kindly. They have become like the world’s rubbish and the dirt everyone wipes off.
verseByVerse.theology:
Realized Eschatology and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Corinthians’ problem was not merely social pride but theological confusion about which age they were in. They were living as if the resurrection age had fully arrived — treating this present life as the time of reigning and riches. Paul’s corrective is eschatological: we are still in the “between the times,” the age between the first and second coming, in which the pattern of the Christian life is cruciform, not triumphant. The “not yet” of eschatology shapes the “how” of Christian living. Suffering, weakness, and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but participation in Christ’s own pattern — the pattern of resurrection that comes through, not around, the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman spectacle of condemned criminals paraded before the crowd before their execution is the image behind v. 9 (“a spectacle to the world”). Paul uses the imagery of the arena: God has made the apostles last, like the condemned criminals brought on at the end of the show. This was not hyperbole; Paul had been beaten, imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the contemporary version of Corinthian triumphalism: the claim that health, wealth, and success are the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s fools for Christ’s sake, hungry and homeless, are a permanent rebuke to any theology that makes suffering an anomaly rather than a participation in the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!

Already you have all you want! Key words. Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come. “All you want” (korennymi, to be full, satiated). They felt satisfied, spiritually full.

Already you have become rich! Key words. Rich in gifts and knowledge (1:5), and proud of it.

Without us you have become kings! Key words. They behaved as if they were already reigning, as believers will in the age to come (6:2–3; Revelation 5:10), and without needing the apostles. This is sometimes called over-realised eschatology: claiming now the glory that belongs to the future.

And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you! Key words. Paul wishes it were true, because then the apostles’ sufferings would be over too. But it is not yet the time to reign. It is the time to suffer with Christ before being glorified with him (Romans 8:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing now. In Christ we have every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3). But the full glory is future, and the present is marked by the cross.

In a sentence. Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! You have begun to reign, and that without us! How Paul wishes that you really had begun to reign, so that we also might reign with you!

On a Tuesday. Beware of a Christianity that promises everything now: health, wealth, triumph. The crown comes after the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come.

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.

For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all. Key words. “Exhibited” (apodeiknymi, put on display). Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena last for the crowd’s entertainment. The apostles are like those condemned men.

Like men sentenced to death. Key words. “Sentenced to death” (epithanatios, condemned to die). The apostles lived under constant threat of death (15:30–31; 2 Corinthians 4:11).

Because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men. Key words. “Spectacle” (theatron, theatre, show). The whole universe, visible and invisible, watches the apostles suffer. They are the show in the arena.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God despises his apostles. He displays through their weakness the power of the cross (2 Corinthians 4:7–10; 12:9–10).

In a sentence. For it seems to Paul that God has put us apostles on display at the end of the procession, like those condemned to die in the arena. We have been made a spectacle to the whole universe, to angels as well as to human beings.

For worship. Angels are watching how Christians suffer. Ask God to make your suffering a display of his grace.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena at the end of the games.

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.

We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. Key words. Three biting contrasts. The apostles are fools because they preach a foolish message (1:18). The Corinthians think themselves wise.

We are weak, but you are strong. Key words. The apostles are weak (2:3); the Corinthians think they are strong.

You are held in honor, but we in disrepute. Key words. “Disrepute” (atimos, without honour, dishonoured). The Corinthians enjoyed status; the apostles were despised.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians really were wise and strong. Paul is exposing their pride. They had taken on the world’s values.

In a sentence. We are fools for Christ, but you are so wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honoured, we are dishonoured!

On a Tuesday. If following Christ costs you reputation, you are walking where the apostles walked.

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.

To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless. Key words. Not a past phase but the present reality. Hunger, thirst, ragged clothes, beatings (kolaphizō, struck with the fist, as Jesus was, Matthew 26:67), no settled home.

And we labor, working with our own hands. Key words. Paul worked as a tentmaker to support himself (Acts 18:3; 20:34). Greeks thought manual work was beneath a philosopher. Paul accepted it so as not to burden anyone (9:12).

When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. Key words. The way of Jesus (Luke 6:28; 1 Peter 2:23). Reviled (insulted): bless. Persecuted: endure. Slandered: entreat (parakaleō, speak kindly, appeal).

We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things. Key words. “Scum” (perikatharma, what is wiped off when cleaning, filth) and “refuse” (peripsēma, scrapings, dirt). Both words were also used of the lowest criminals, sometimes sacrificed to purge a city in time of disaster. The apostles are treated as human garbage.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be homeless or poor. It means that faithfulness to Christ can cost everything, and apostolic ministry did.

In a sentence. To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are in rags, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. We work hard with our own hands. When we are cursed, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; when we are slandered, we answer kindly. We have become the scum of the earth, the garbage of the world, right up to this moment.

For worship. Thank God for those who have suffered to bring you the gospel. Pray for persecuted Christians today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he is not writing to shame them but to warn them as his dear children. They may have countless guardians in Christ, but they do not have many fathers; through the gospel Paul became their father in Christ Jesus. So he urges them to imitate him. That is why he is sending Timothy, his loved and faithful son in the Lord, to remind them of his way of life in Christ, which he teaches in every church. Some have become arrogant, as though Paul were not coming. But he will come soon, if the Lord wills, and find out not what these proud people say but what power they have, because God’s kingdom is not a matter of talk but of power. Which do they want: that he come with a rod, or with love and a gentle spirit?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fatherhood of the Apostle and Spiritual Formation by Imitation

Paul’s claim to spiritual fatherhood over the Corinthian church is grounded in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The new birth produces a spiritual parentage — and the one through whose proclamation the Spirit brought new birth to a community is, in a real sense, their spiritual father. This is not about control but about formation. Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living embodiment of the gospel he preached — not his person but his pattern, the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had, in Paul’s absence, developed arrogant teachers who had dismissed the apostle. Timothy is sent to embody what Paul had taught by his life — because argument alone, without the living example, is insufficient. Now: The pastoral call to “be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1) is the most demanding thing a minister can say — and the most necessary. Disciples need models, not merely doctrines. The church that produces only correct theology without cruciform character has missed the point of the apostolic office.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. Key words. Paul softens his tone. His irony is not to humiliate them but to warn (noutheteō, admonish, counsel) them, as a father warns his children.

For though you have countless guides in Christ. Key words. “Countless” (literally ten thousand). The word for “guides” (paidagōgoi) was used of the household slave who took children to school and supervised them (Galatians 3:24). Many teachers had come and gone in Corinth.

You do not have many fathers. Key words. Tutors can be hired; a father is unique. Paul’s relationship to them is deeper than any later teacher’s.

For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel. Key words. “Became your father” (gennaō, begot). Through his preaching of the gospel, God gave them new birth. Paul was the instrument of their spiritual birth.

Where Christians differ: calling ministers father. Jesus said to call no one on earth your father (Matthew 23:9), yet Paul calls himself their father. Some use this to justify the title Father for priests. Verdict: Jesus forbade giving any human the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs only to God. Paul is describing a relationship, not claiming a title or rank. He brought them to new birth through the gospel, and cares for them with a father’s love (1 Thessalonians 2:11). The word describes affection and responsibility, not a priestly office.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul has authority over their faith in place of Christ (2 Corinthians 1:24). He is a father in Christ, through the gospel.

In a sentence. Paul is writing this not to shame you but to warn you as his dear children. Even if you had ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers, for in Christ Jesus he became your father through the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have helped bring to faith or grow in Christ? Care for them like a parent: with warmth, patience and honest warning.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guides” was used of the household slave who took charge of children on their way to school.

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.

I urge you, then, be imitators of me. Key words. “Imitators” (mimētai, from which mimic). Children learn by copying their father. Imitate Paul’s life of cross-shaped humility, the life just described in verses 9–13, not the Corinthians’ pride. Later he adds: as I am of Christ (11:1).

That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. Key words. Timothy, Paul’s spiritual son (1 Timothy 1:2), was on his way to Corinth (16:10). He would be a living example of Paul’s ways.

To remind you of my ways in Christ. Key words. “Ways” (hodoi, paths): Paul’s manner of life and teaching, his patterns as a Christian.

As I teach them everywhere in every church. Key words. Paul did not have special teaching for Corinth. He taught the same things in all the churches (7:17; 11:16; 14:33). Corinth must not think itself an exception.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was arrogant or sinless. He calls them to imitate his imitation of Christ.

In a sentence. Therefore Paul urges you to imitate him. For this reason he has sent to you Timothy, his son whom he loves, who is faithful in the Lord. He will remind you of his way of life in Christ Jesus, which agrees with what he teaches everywhere in every church.

For worship. Thank God for the Christians whose lives you can imitate. Pray that your life would be worth imitating.

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.

Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. Key words. “Arrogant” (physioō, puffed up). Some had been saying Paul would not dare return; he sends letters and Timothy, but stays away. So they felt free to ignore him.

But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. Key words. Paul does intend to come (16:5). “If the Lord wills”: a good habit, recognising God’s control of our plans (James 4:15).

And I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. Key words. Talk (logos, word): impressive speech, the very thing Corinth prized. Power (dynamis): the real working of God’s Spirit in a life. Paul will test whether their talk has any spiritual reality behind it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words are unimportant. Paul’s ministry was a ministry of the word. But words without the Spirit’s power are empty.

In a sentence. Some of you have become arrogant, as if Paul were not coming to you. But he will come to you very soon, if the Lord is willing, and then he will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.

On a Tuesday. Does your life have real spiritual power behind your words: love, patience, holiness? Ask God for it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?

For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. Key words. The kingdom of God is God’s rule, present now through Christ and the Spirit. It shows itself not in eloquent religious talk but in changed lives (Romans 14:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:5).

What do you wish? Key words. The choice is theirs.

Shall I come to you with a rod. Key words. A father’s rod of discipline (Proverbs 13:24). Paul has authority to discipline, as chapter 5 shows.

Or with love in a spirit of gentleness? Key words. Gentleness (prautēs, meekness, mildness). Paul prefers gentleness. Notice that both the rod and gentleness are love; but gentleness is what he longs to use. Whether he can depends on their repentance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that discipline is unloving. Loving fathers discipline (Hebrews 12:6). But they prefer to see children respond to gentleness.

In a sentence. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. What do you prefer? Shall Paul come to you with a rod of discipline, or shall he come in love and with a gentle spirit?

For worship. Respond to God’s gentle correction quickly, so that he need not use the rod.
