11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapters 11–14 deal with problems in the church’s gatherings. The first concerns how men and women appear when they pray or prophesy. In the Roman world clothing and hair sent strong signals. A respectable married woman covered her head in public with a veil or the fold of her mantle; going uncovered could suggest immodesty or rebellion, and shaving a woman’s head was a mark of disgrace. Men, by contrast, did not cover their heads, except in some pagan rituals where Roman priests sacrificed with the toga drawn over the head. Some Corinthian women, perhaps reasoning that in Christ distinctions no longer mattered, were praying and prophesying uncovered. Paul grounds his answer in creation and in the order of headship, God, Christ, man, woman, while insisting that in the Lord men and women depend on each other.

The second problem was worse. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared evening meal in a wealthy member’s house. The host’s friends reclined in the small dining room and ate the best food early; latecomers, often slaves who had worked all day, crowded into the courtyard with little or nothing. Some went hungry while others got drunk. Paul says this is not the Lord’s Supper at all. He repeats the account of the Last Supper that he received from the Lord, reminds them that the meal proclaims Christ’s death until he returns, and warns that eating in an unworthy way, despising Christ’s body, brings judgement. They must examine themselves and wait for one another.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to follow his example as he follows Christ’s, and praises them for holding to the traditions he passed on. But he wants them to understand that Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. A man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head, and a woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours hers; it is as shameful as having her head shaved, so if she will not cover it she might as well cut off her hair. A man should not cover his head, since he is God’s image and glory, while the woman is the glory of man, for woman came from man and was created for him. So a woman should have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels. Yet in the Lord neither is independent of the other: woman came from man, but every man is born of woman, and everything comes from God. Paul asks them to judge for themselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray uncovered, and points to nature: long hair is a disgrace to a man but a glory to a woman, given her as a covering. If anyone wants to argue, the churches of God have no other practice.
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, Order, and the Trinity

Paul’s grounding of the male-female relationship in the Father-Son relationship (v. 3) is one of the most important and most debated texts in trinitarian theology. If “the head of Christ is God” describes an eternal subordination within the Godhead, it supports a permanent hierarchical ordering of human relationships. Most Reformed theologians have understood this as describing the economic Trinity (the Son’s voluntary submission in the incarnation and redemption) rather than ontological subordination within the immanent Trinity. Either way, Paul is using the divine relational order as the theological model for the ordering of human relationships in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific head covering practice was an expression of propriety and social order in a particular cultural context. A woman praying with her head uncovered may have signalled sexual availability or a rejection of the social ordering that the community needed to maintain for the sake of its witness. Now: The head covering practice is not directly applicable in most modern Western contexts. The underlying principle — that worship should reflect an ordered dignity appropriate to the God being worshipped, and that the differentiation of male and female is a gift to be honoured rather than erased — continues to speak into contemporary debates about gender in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s call to imitate him concludes chapter 10: he gives up his rights as Christ did.

The end of chapter 10. This verse belongs with what goes before: Paul gives up his rights as Christ did. Chapter divisions were added in the thirteenth century.

As I am of Christ. Paul is a pattern only as he copies Christ. Imitation of any leader stops where he stops following Christ.

On a Tuesday. Who are you imitating? And who might be imitating you?

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul commends them for holding to the traditions he handed on.

Traditions. Paradoseis: teaching handed down from the apostles, such as the gospel (15:3) and the Lord’s Supper (11:23). Not human customs added to Scripture, but apostolic teaching, now preserved in Scripture.

Tradition and Scripture. Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that apostolic tradition is passed on both in Scripture and in the church’s unwritten tradition. Verdict: the Reformed principle of sola Scriptura: the apostles’ teaching has come down to us in the New Testament, which is the only infallible rule. Church traditions can be valuable but must be tested by Scripture.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “brothers”. The earliest lack it.

On a Tuesday. Hold firmly to the apostles’ teaching in your Bible, even when it is unfashionable.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grounds order in worship in a pattern of headship: God the head of Christ, Christ of every man, the husband of his wife.

Head. Kephalē. What does it mean?

“Source” or “origin”, like the head of a river. Egalitarian Christians often take it this way: man is the source of woman (Genesis 2:22), as Christ is the source of the church.

“Authority” or “leadership”, as in Ephesians 5:23 and in the Greek Old Testament, where “head” often means leader (Judges 11:11).

Verdict: authority, with the sense of loving leadership. The order “God is the head of Christ” shows that headship does not mean inferiority: the Son is equal to the Father in nature yet gladly submits to his will. So man and woman are equal in dignity and value, both made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), with different roles in marriage and in the church. This is the complementarian view.

Man and woman, husband and wife. The Greek words can mean either. Paul is probably thinking mainly of husbands and wives, since veils marked married women.

On a Tuesday. Husbands: headship means serving like Christ, not ruling like a tyrant. Wives: respecting your husband’s leadership is not losing your worth, any more than the Son loses his deity by obeying the Father.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife.”

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men and women honour or dishonour their heads by how they appear when praying or prophesying in worship.

Praying and prophesying. In the gathered church. Women did pray and prophesy aloud in worship, fulfilling Joel’s promise: “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17; 21:9).

How does this fit 14:34? In 14:34 women are to “keep silent” in the churches. Since Paul here allows women to pray and prophesy, the silence must be specific: probably the weighing of prophecies or authoritative teaching (1 Timothy 2:12). This is the complementarian reading.

Dishonours his head. Both his own head and his “head”, Christ (v. 3). For a man, covering may have looked like a pagan priest at sacrifice, with his toga pulled over his head.

Shaved. In the ancient world a shaved head could be a mark of shame for a woman, perhaps a punishment for adultery.

On a Tuesday. Women who pray aloud in church gatherings are doing something Paul assumes. Encourage them.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and married status. Christians differ on how the principle applies today.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An uncovered woman in that culture brought shame, and man is the image and glory of God, woman the glory of man.

Logic. Being uncovered was as shameful as being shaved. If she would not accept one, she should not do the other.

Image and glory. From Genesis 1:26–27. Man reflects God’s glory as his representative. Paul does not deny that woman is also God’s image (Genesis 1:27 says both are); his point is about the order of creation in Genesis 2.

Woman the glory of man. She is his honour, his crown (Proverbs 12:4). Not inferior, but the one who brings him honour.

On a Tuesday. A husband should treat his wife as his glory: speak well of her, honour her publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul grounds the distinction in the order of creation.

Genesis 2. “The rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman” (Genesis 2:22). And God said, “I will make him a helper fit for him” (Genesis 2:18). The word “helper” is often used of God himself (Psalm 33:20), so it implies no inferiority.

Creation, not culture. Paul grounds his argument in creation, which is why complementarians see the principle as lasting, not merely Corinthian custom.

On a Tuesday. God designed men and women differently, to complete each other. Celebrate the differences.

parallels.desc: a helper fit for him; she shall be called Woman

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman’s head covering is a sign of authority, because of the angels.

Symbol of authority. Literally “authority on her head”. Either a sign of her husband’s authority over her, or a sign of her own authority to pray and prophesy in worship. Verdict: probably both: the covering showed she respected the created order, and so had the right to take part.

Because of the angels. One of the Bible’s puzzling phrases.

Angels are present at worship (the Dead Sea Scrolls say so), and watch for proper order (Ephesians 3:10; 1 Timothy 5:21).

Some ancient readers linked it with the “sons of God” in Genesis 6:2, fallen angels attracted to women. This seems unlikely.

Verdict: the first: angels watch the church’s worship, and respect for God’s order honours them and God.

On a Tuesday. Worship is watched by heaven. Come with reverence.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present at worship and to guard God’s order.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Lord, man and woman are mutually dependent, and all things come from God.

Mutual dependence. Paul guards against any idea that men are superior. Every man owes his life to a mother.

In the Lord. In Christ, men and women are equal heirs (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7, “heirs with you of the grace of life”).

All things from God. Both sexes, and their differences, are God’s good design.

On a Tuesday. In your church and home, value men and women alike, and depend on each other.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nature itself teaches a difference between men and women.

Nature. Physis: the natural order of things as people sense it. Most cultures distinguish men and women by hair and dress, though the details vary.

Long hair. In Greek and Roman culture men usually wore short hair; long hair on a man could suggest effeminacy. Nazirites in Israel grew their hair as a special vow (Numbers 6:5), so Paul is not making an absolute rule.

Hair as covering. Some argue that a woman’s long hair is itself the covering, so no veil is required. But the argument of verses 5–6 seems to assume a covering in addition to hair.

Do head coverings bind today?

Some Christians (Brethren, some Reformed, Anabaptist and Orthodox churches) practise head coverings for women in worship as a lasting command.

Most Christians hold that the principle, honouring God’s created order of men and women, is lasting, while the form, a veil, expressed it in that culture.

Verdict: the second, held charitably. Paul appeals to custom and nature as well as creation, and veiling carried meanings in Corinth that it does not carry in most Western cultures. But women who choose to cover their heads in worship should be respected, and churches should find ways to honour the distinction between men and women.

On a Tuesday. In your own culture, how can men and women dress and present themselves in worship in ways that honour God and do not distract others?

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the churches follow this practice.

Contentious. Paul does not want an endless argument. This was the practice of all the churches.

No such practice. No custom of women praying uncovered.

On a Tuesday. On secondary matters, avoid becoming contentious. Follow your church’s practice unless it contradicts Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Paul has no praise for them, because their meetings do more harm than good. He hears that when they gather there are divisions, and he partly believes it; there have to be differences, so that those who are genuine stand out. When they meet, it is not really the Lord’s Supper they eat, because each person goes ahead with his own meal, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk. Do they not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do they despise God’s church and humiliate those who have nothing? Paul will certainly not praise them for this.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Enacted Gospel Equality

Paul’s critique of the Corinthian Supper is grounded in his theology of the cross. The Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26) — the death in which the rich Son of God became poor for the sake of the poor, in which the Lord washed his disciples’ feet, in which social distinctions were overcome in the one body given for all. A Supper that reinforces social stratification is not merely socially unkind; it is a contradiction of what is being enacted. The body and blood of Christ at the table cannot be participated in rightly by those who simultaneously despise the members of his body gathered around the table.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The patronage culture of Roman Corinth structured even the shared meal around social hierarchy: the wealthy ate better food in the inner room; clients and dependents got lesser portions in the outer rooms. The Corinthians had imported this structure wholesale into the church’s gathering. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the place where the social equalisations of the gospel are most visibly enacted — or most visibly denied. The church where wealth, race, or education creates a gradient of welcome and participation has committed the Corinthian error at its most fundamental level.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their gatherings are doing more harm than good, because of divisions.

Not for the better. A shocking verdict: their worship made them worse.

Divisions. Not the factions of chapter 1 but social divisions: rich and poor at the table.

Factions. Haireseis, from which we get “heresy”, originally “choices” or “parties”. Irony: the divisions expose who is truly approved.

On a Tuesday. Is your church gathering better for everyone who comes? Or do some leave feeling more excluded?

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their selfish feasts, where some go hungry and others get drunk, are not the Lord’s Supper.

The setting. Churches met in homes of wealthier members, such as Gaius, “who is host to me and to the whole church” (Romans 16:23). A Roman villa had a dining room (triclinium) holding perhaps nine to twelve reclining guests, and a courtyard (atrium) where others would stand or sit. A villa excavated at Corinth has just such a layout.

Social custom. At Roman banquets hosts often served different food to guests of different rank. The writer Pliny the Younger complained of a dinner where the host served fine food to himself and his friends and cheap food to lesser guests. The Corinthian church brought this custom into the Lord’s Supper.

Each his own meal. The wealthy, free to come early, ate their own food. Slaves and labourers arrived late, after work, to find little left.

Despise the church. To humiliate poor believers is to despise God’s people, for whom Christ died.

On a Tuesday. At church lunches, notice who is sitting alone. Do the wealthy and confident cluster together? Make room at your table.
verseByVerse.note: The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal. The wealthy, free to arrive early, ate and drank before poorer members — often slaves — could come after work.

parallels.desc: your love feasts

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul passes on what he received from the Lord. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me.” After supper he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; whenever you drink it, do this in remembrance of me.” Every time they eat this bread and drink this cup, they proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. So anyone who eats or drinks in an unworthy way will be guilty of sinning against the Lord’s body and blood. Each person should examine himself before eating and drinking, because whoever eats and drinks without recognising the body eats and drinks judgement on himself. That is why many of them are weak and sick, and some have died. If they judged themselves properly, they would not come under judgement. When the Lord judges, he disciplines them so that they will not be condemned with the world. So when they gather to eat, they must wait for one another. Anyone who is hungry should eat at home, so that their meetings do not lead to judgement. Paul will give further instructions when he comes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Real Presence and the Reformed Understanding of the Supper

Calvin’s eucharistic theology, developed precisely in dialogue with this passage, insisted on a genuine but spiritual presence of Christ in the Supper — against both the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (physical transformation of the elements) and Zwingli’s pure memorialism (the Supper as merely symbolic). Paul’s language of “participation” (10:16) and “proclaiming the Lord’s death” (11:26) supports a real, active, communicative presence of Christ at the table — where Christ genuinely gives himself to be received by faith, and where genuine nourishment of the soul takes place through the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian abuse of the Supper — reducing it to a social meal stratified by class — was the practical outworking of their failure to grasp the gospel. When you understand that Christ died equally for the rich and the poor in your community, you cannot eat well while they starve at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the church’s most powerful enacted proclamation of the gospel — which is why its abuse is so serious, and why its right practice (the community gathered equally around the cross) is so significant as a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hands on what he received from the Lord: Jesus’ words over the bread on the night he was betrayed.

Received and delivered. Technical terms for passing on tradition (15:3). Paul received it ultimately from the Lord, probably through the apostles in Jerusalem. This letter (around AD 54) contains the earliest written account of the Last Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

The night he was betrayed. Or “handed over”, both by Judas and by the Father (Romans 8:32). The Supper is set in the shadow of the cross.

This is my body. See the four views on 10:16. Jesus spoke while present in his body, holding bread; the disciples did not think they were eating his flesh. The Reformed view: the bread signifies and seals his body given for us, and by faith we feed on Christ.

In remembrance. Anamnēsis: not merely recalling a past event, but making it present in worship, as Israel remembered the exodus at Passover.

Is the Supper a sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching calls the Mass a sacrifice, making present Christ’s one sacrifice. Verdict: the Supper is a remembrance of a sacrifice, not a sacrifice itself. “We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). Our offering in the Supper is praise and ourselves (Romans 12:1).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read “Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you.” The earliest lack “Take, eat” and “broken”; these were added from the Gospels and from liturgical use. John 19:36 notes that none of his bones was broken.

For worship. At the Supper, remember Jesus on the night he was betrayed. He gave thanks.
verseByVerse.note: This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup is the new covenant in Christ’s blood, to be drunk in remembrance of him.

After supper. At Passover, the third cup, “the cup of blessing”, was drunk after the main meal.

The new covenant. Jeremiah 31:31: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant.” Sealed with blood, as the old covenant was at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

As often. How often should Christians take the Supper? The early church seems to have done so weekly (Acts 20:7). Calvin wanted weekly communion, though the magistrates of Geneva would not allow it. Churches today vary from weekly to quarterly. Verdict: Scripture gives no fixed rule, but frequent communion is the better pattern.

On a Tuesday. Remember that you are in a covenant with God, sealed in Christ’s blood. Live in its promises today.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every celebration of the Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes.

Proclaim. The Supper is itself a sermon: a visible word, as Augustine called it. It announces the gospel.

Until he comes. The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the return, to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

For worship. The Supper is the church’s announcement to the world: Christ died, and he is coming again.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To eat in an unworthy manner is to sin against the Lord’s body and blood.

An unworthy manner. Not “unworthy people”. No one is worthy in himself. Paul means the way they were eating: greedily, drunkenly, despising the poor. The note in the ESV text agrees.

Guilty. Treating the Supper with contempt is like taking sides with those who crucified the Lord.

What it does not mean. Many sensitive believers have stayed away from the Lord’s Table for fear of being unworthy. That misreads the verse. The Table is for sinners who trust Christ and want to follow him. The warning is for those who treat it carelessly or come while despising their brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. If you feel unworthy to take communion, you are exactly the kind of person it is for. Come, trusting Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating — despising the poor — not to whether the individual was worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each believer should examine himself before eating.

Examine. Dokimazō: test. Ask honestly: do I trust Christ? Is there unconfessed sin? Am I at odds with a brother or sister (Matthew 5:23–24)?

And so eat. Not “and so stay away”. The goal of self-examination is to come.

Fencing the table. Many Reformed churches give a warning before communion, inviting all who trust Christ and are members in good standing of a church, and warning those living in unrepentant sin. This is a right application of Paul’s words.

On a Tuesday. If you will take communion this Sunday, spend a few minutes on Saturday evening examining yourself, confessing sin and seeking to put things right with anyone you have wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eating without discerning the body brings judgment.

Discerning the body. Two readings:

Recognising the Lord’s body in the bread, that is, treating the Supper as sacred.

Recognising the church as Christ’s body (10:17; 12:12–27), that is, treating fellow believers rightly.

Verdict: the second fits the context of rich and poor best: the Corinthians were ignoring the body of believers. But the two cannot be separated: those who honour Christ’s body given for them will honour his body, the church.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “eateth and drinketh unworthily … not discerning the Lord’s body”) add “unworthily” and “the Lord’s”. The earliest read simply “without discerning the body”.

On a Tuesday. You cannot love Christ and despise his people. Before communion, ask whom in the church you have been ignoring.
verseByVerse.note: “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as his body.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s discipline has fallen on them, to keep them from being condemned with the world.

Illness and death. Paul sees God’s discipline in illness and deaths in Corinth. Like Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).

What it does not mean. Not that every illness is punishment for sin (John 9:3). Paul knows of this specific case through prophetic insight. We should not assume a sick believer is being judged.

Disciplined. Paideuometha: trained like children. God’s judgement on his people is fatherly discipline, “for the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6), aimed at saving them, not condemning them.

Not condemned with the world. Even those who died were not lost; their discipline kept them from final condemnation.

On a Tuesday. If you are going through hardship, ask whether God is calling you to repentance; but do not assume it is punishment. God’s discipline is always loving.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must wait for one another and keep private meals for home.

Wait. Ekdechesthe: wait for, or welcome. Share the meal together.

Eat at home. If you are hungry, have something before you come. The church meal is about fellowship, not filling up.

The rest. Paul will sort out other details in person. We do not know what they were.

On a Tuesday. At church gatherings, put others first: wait, share, welcome.

For worship. Thank God for the Lord’s Supper: Christ’s body given, his blood shed, his people made one, his return proclaimed.

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. The Corinthians were especially impressed by dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, and treated them as marks of superior spirituality. Their pagan background explains some of this. Greek religion prized ecstatic experience: the prophetess at Delphi spoke in a trance, and the worship of Dionysus involved frenzy. Being carried away was taken as a sign of the divine. Paul begins with a test that has nothing to do with excitement: the Spirit always leads people to confess that Jesus is Lord.

Then he insists that the gifts are many but the giver is one, the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God, and that every gift is given for the good of the whole church, not for individual display. He uses the familiar picture of the body, a common image in ancient politics for a community whose members must cooperate. In Corinth the picture had a local twist: at the temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, worshippers left clay models of the body parts they wanted healed, hands, feet, eyes, ears, and many have been dug up. Paul says the church is one body with many parts, all baptised by one Spirit. No member can say it does not belong, and none can say it does not need the others; the weaker parts are indispensable, and all share suffering and honour. God has placed gifts in the church as he chose, and not everyone has the same gift. They should seek the greater gifts, and Paul is about to show them a better way still, the way of love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not want them to be ignorant about spiritual gifts. They remember that as pagans they were swept along and led off to speechless idols. So he gives a test: no one speaking by God’s Spirit says “Jesus is cursed”, and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit. There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit; different kinds of service, but the same Lord; different kinds of working, but the same God works all of them in everyone. To each person the Spirit is shown in some way for the common good. To one the Spirit gives a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another faith, to another gifts of healing, to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish spirits, to another different kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes them to each person as he decides.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

The explicit trinitarianism of vv. 4–6 is remarkable as a casual structural feature of Paul’s argument: he assumes the Trinity without arguing for it. Reformed pneumatology has always grounded the discussion of spiritual gifts in this trinitarian framework: the gifts are not the Spirit’s autonomous productions but the common work of Father, Son, and Spirit. This prevents both the elevation of the Spirit over Christ (a common charismatic error) and the neglect of the Spirit’s ongoing work (a temptation in cessationist circles): all genuine gifts are simultaneously the work of the triune God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian believers were apparently competing for the most impressive gifts, using spiritual gifts as social capital. Paul’s trinitarian grounding removes the competition from its foundation: you cannot boast in a gift that was sovereignly given to you by the Spirit who gives as he wills. Now: The same gift-competitive dynamic operates in charismatic and Reformed communities alike, in different directions: charismatics sometimes elevate dramatic gifts (tongues, healing) over quiet ones; cessationists sometimes elevate intellectual gifts (teaching, wisdom) over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both hierarchies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wants them to understand spiritual gifts, remembering how they were once led astray by idols.

Spiritual gifts. Pneumatika: literally “spiritual things” or “spiritual people”. The Corinthians’ word, perhaps. Paul soon switches to charismata, “gifts of grace” (v. 4), stressing that they are gifts, not achievements.

Led astray. In pagan worship people were swept away by powerful religious experiences, emotional or ecstatic. Paul reminds them that such experiences led them to “speechless idols” (Habakkuk 2:18), gods that could not speak at all.

The point. Intensity of experience is no proof of the Holy Spirit. Pagans had it too.

On a Tuesday. Do not judge a church or a meeting by how emotional or exciting it is. Ask whether Christ is being honoured.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit leads people to confess Jesus as Lord, never to curse him.

“Jesus is accursed.” Who would say that? Suggestions: Jewish opponents applying Deuteronomy 21:23 (“a hanged man is cursed by God”) to Jesus; Roman officials demanding that Christians curse Christ, as Pliny later did; people in ecstatic states; or, according to some, early Gnostics who separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ. Or Paul may be giving a deliberately extreme example. Verdict: we do not know if anyone in Corinth said it. The point is the test: whatever speaks against Jesus is not of the Spirit.

“Jesus is Lord.” The earliest Christian creed (Romans 10:9, “if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord”). Not just saying the words, but genuinely confessing his lordship. Only the Spirit can bring a person to that.

The test of every gift. Does it exalt Jesus as Lord? “Test the spirits” (1 John 4:1–3).

On a Tuesday. If you truly confess Jesus as Lord, the Spirit is at work in you, whether or not you have spectacular gifts.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are many gifts, services and activities, but one Spirit, one Lord and one God.

The Trinity. Spirit, Lord (Christ) and God (the Father). The variety of gifts flows from the unity of the triune God.

Gifts, service, activities. Three words for the same things seen from different angles: gifts of grace (charismata), forms of service (diakoniai), effects of God’s power (energēmata). Every gift is a form of service.

On a Tuesday. Your gift may be quiet, like serving tea or visiting the sick. It comes from the same triune God as the most visible gift.
verseByVerse.note: Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every believer is given some gift for the common good.

To each. Every believer has a gift (Ephesians 4:7; 1 Peter 4:10). No passengers.

Manifestation. The gift shows the Spirit’s presence.

For the common good. The purpose of every gift: to build up others, not to show off. “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another” (1 Peter 4:10).

On a Tuesday. Ask: what gift has God given me, and how can I use it for others this week?

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit gives wisdom, knowledge and faith to different believers.

Word of wisdom, word of knowledge. The Corinthians’ favourite words (1:5; 8:1). Probably gifts of teaching: wise application of God’s truth and insight into its meaning. Some modern charismatic teaching treats a “word of knowledge” as supernatural information about a stranger (an illness, a secret). Verdict: Paul gives no definition; in the context of the letter, “wisdom” and “knowledge” relate to understanding the gospel (2:6–13). The modern usage reads more into the words than the text gives.

Faith. Not saving faith, which every believer has, but a special confidence in God for great things (13:2, “faith, so as to remove mountains”).

Gifts of healing. Plural: different healings. Given to the apostles and others in the early church (Acts 3:6–8; 5:15–16; James 5:14–15).

A textual note. Some manuscripts read “by the same Spirit” rather than “by the one Spirit” in verse 9. The meaning is the same.

On a Tuesday. If someone in your church has a gift for explaining the Bible wisely, encourage them to use it.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one Spirit gives each gift as he wills.

Prophecy. Speaking a message from God (14:1–5, 24–25). Discussed fully in chapter 14.

Distinguishing spirits. Discerning whether a prophecy or spiritual manifestation is from God, from a human source, or from evil spirits.

Tongues. What were they?

Real human languages the speaker had not learned, as at Pentecost: “how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?” (Acts 2:8).

Ecstatic speech or a heavenly prayer language, “the tongues of angels” (13:1).

Verdict: the same word is used in Acts 2, where tongues were real languages, and “kinds of tongues” suggests languages. But Paul does allow that tongues may sometimes be unknown to any hearer and need interpretation (14:2).

As he wills. The Spirit chooses. No one can demand a particular gift.

Do these gifts continue today? Christians hold three main positions.

Pentecostals: all the gifts continue, and speaking in tongues is the normal evidence of being baptised in the Spirit.

Continuationists (such as Wayne Grudem and many charismatic Reformed believers): all the gifts may continue, though prophecy today is not equal to Scripture and must be tested.

Cessationists (such as B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin): the revelatory and sign gifts, apostleship, prophecy, tongues and miraculous healing, belonged to the foundation of the church and ceased with the apostles, while God still heals and works wonders in answer to prayer as he wills.

Verdict: the cessationist view, held with respect for brothers and sisters who differ. The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Miraculous signs confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). With Scripture complete, we have no need of new revelation. Yet all sides agree on Paul’s main point: every gift is from the Spirit, for the common good, and less important than love.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your view of the gifts, ask whether your gift is being used in love for others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The body is one, though it has many parts, and so it is with Christ. All believers, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, were baptised by one Spirit into one body and were all given the one Spirit to drink. The body is not one part but many. If the foot said it does not belong because it is not a hand, it would still belong; if the ear said it does not belong because it is not an eye, it would still belong. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell? God has placed each part in the body just as he wanted. If all were one part, there would be no body. As it is, there are many parts but one body. The eye cannot tell the hand it does not need it, nor the head the feet. In fact the parts that seem weaker are essential, the parts we think less honourable we treat with more honour, and our less presentable parts are treated with more modesty, while the presentable ones need no special care. God has put the body together, giving greater honour to the parts that lacked it, so that there should be no division in the body, but its parts should care equally for each other. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part shares its joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Ecclesiology and Soteriology United

Paul’s body metaphor is not merely sociological (a useful way to describe community life) but soteriological: the church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised all believers into the one body of the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real — not metaphorical — which is why the suffering of one member is genuinely felt by the whole (v. 26). The theology of the body of Christ is the foundation of Paul’s entire ethic of community: you cannot be indifferent to the suffering of a fellow member of Christ’s body any more than your left hand can be indifferent to the pain in your right foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had produced both contempt (the tongues-speakers dismissing those with lesser gifts) and despair (those with lesser gifts feeling excluded). Paul’s body metaphor addresses both directly: the despairers are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church community has its impressive and its unimpressive members by the world’s standards. Paul’s insight is that the one who seems indispensable and the one who seems marginal are both placed by the same God — and the functioning of the body requires both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is one body with many members, baptised by one Spirit into one body.

So it is with Christ. Not “so it is with the church”, but “with Christ”. The church is so united to Christ that it can be called by his name.

Baptised by one Spirit. When does this happen?

Pentecostal teaching: baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by tongues.

The Reformed and most evangelical view: every believer is baptised by the Spirit into Christ’s body at conversion.

Verdict: the second. Paul says “we all” were baptised by the Spirit, including those who did not speak in tongues (v. 30). Believers may later receive fresh fillings of the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), but the baptism of the Spirit is what makes a person a Christian (Romans 8:9).

Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. The deepest divisions of the ancient world overcome (Galatians 3:28).

Drink one Spirit. Like water poured out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37–39).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “made to drink into one Spirit”) add “into”. The earliest lack it.

On a Tuesday. The person at church you find hardest to like was baptised by the same Spirit into the same body. Treat them as part of yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No member may think it does not belong because it is different.

The body image. Familiar in the ancient world. The Roman historian Livy tells how, when the common people of Rome went on strike, the consul Menenius Agrippa told them a fable of the limbs rebelling against the belly: when they refused to feed it, they all wasted away. The image was usually used to tell lower classes to stay in their place. Paul uses it to honour the weaker parts.

Feeling left out. The foot and the ear envy the hand and the eye. Some Corinthians without showy gifts felt they did not belong.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you have nothing to offer your church, you are wrong. You belong.
verseByVerse.note: The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united community.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A body made of one part could not function.

Variety is essential. A church where everyone had the same gift, such as tongues, would be a monster.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for church members who are not like you.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has arranged each member exactly as he chose.

God arranged. Your place in the church is God’s decision, not an accident.

On a Tuesday. Instead of wishing for another person’s gift, ask how to use yours where God has placed you.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
No member may think it does not need the others.

Pride. Now the opposite problem: the gifted looking down on others. The eye and the head were thought of as the noblest parts.

On a Tuesday. Preachers need the people who set up chairs. Leaders need those who pray quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weaker and less honoured members are indispensable.

Weaker but indispensable. The heart, lungs and liver are hidden and fragile, but you cannot live without them.

Less honourable parts. We cover parts of the body with clothing out of modesty, giving them honour.

God gives honour. God’s way reverses human ranking (1:26–28).

Corinth’s healing temple. In the Asclepion at Corinth, worshippers left clay models of the parts they wanted healed: limbs, eyes, ears, genitals. Paul’s first readers might have pictured these detached parts. In Christ’s body no part is detached or discarded.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church is “weaker”: the elderly, the disabled, the shy, people with dementia? Give them special honour. They are indispensable.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made the body so that its members care for one another, suffering and rejoicing together.

No division. Schisma, as in 1:10. God designed the body to prevent division.

Same care. Mutual concern, not ranking.

Suffer and rejoice together. “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). When you stub your toe, your whole body feels it.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone in your church suffering? Feel it with them: visit, call, pray. Is someone being honoured? Celebrate with them, without envy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them plainly that they are Christ’s body, and each one of them is a part of it. God has placed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and different kinds of tongues. Are all apostles, prophets or teachers? Do all work miracles, have gifts of healing, speak in tongues or interpret? Obviously not. So they should eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now Paul will show them the most excellent way of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The list of gifts in vv. 28–30, with its implied ordering (first, second, third), suggests that Paul does see a hierarchy of value in gifts — not because some are intrinsically superior but because some are more directly edifying for the whole community. Apostles and prophets lay the doctrinal foundation; teachers expound it; the other gifts serve the body in various ways. But the “still more excellent way” of chapter 13 is not a further gift above tongues and prophecy; it is the character quality that makes the exercise of any gift genuinely excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had inverted the hierarchy: tongues (the most self-focused gift in Paul’s analysis) was being treated as the most prestigious. Paul’s list puts tongues last. The correction is not to dismiss tongues but to reorder values: gifts that build the community outrank gifts that edify only the speaker. Now: The principle applies in every community: the gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up the body has missed what gifts are for. The “excellent way” is available to every gift-user who submits his gift to love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are Christ’s body, and God has appointed apostles, prophets, teachers and other gifts.

You are Christ’s body. Not a body, but the body of Christ in Corinth.

First, second, third. A ranking, but by importance for building up the church, not by status. Apostles, prophets and teachers bring God’s word. Tongues come last, deliberately: the Corinthians put them first.

Apostles. The Twelve and Paul, witnesses of the risen Christ with unique authority (9:1; 15:8). Some modern groups appoint “apostles” today; the New Testament office of apostle was not repeatable.

Helping and administrating. Unspectacular gifts, listed among the miraculous ones. Kybernēseis, administration, is the word for steering a ship.

On a Tuesday. Church administration, helping and practical service are gifts of the Spirit as much as healing. Thank the people who do them.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not every member has every gift.

The answer is no. In Greek each question expects “no”. Not every believer speaks in tongues. This answers the teaching that tongues are the necessary sign of Spirit baptism.

On a Tuesday. If you have never spoken in tongues, you are not a second-class Christian. Paul says so.

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They should desire the greater gifts, and Paul will show them the most excellent way.

Desire the higher gifts. Those that build up the church most, especially prophecy and teaching (14:1–5). Some read this as a statement rather than a command (“you are eagerly desiring”), describing their craving for showy gifts. Verdict: it is most likely a command, as in 14:1. Seek gifts that serve others.

A still more excellent way. Not another gift, but love: the way all gifts must be used. Chapter 13 follows.

For worship. Thank God for the variety of gifts in your church, and ask him to fill you with love above all.
