And I will show you a still more excellent way.

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
This famous chapter is often read at weddings, but it was written to rebuke a quarrelsome, proud church that valued spectacular gifts above everything. Paul sets it between his teaching on gifts in chapters 12 and 14, as the “more excellent way” in which every gift must be used. The Greek word for love here, agapē, was rare in ordinary Greek; the Christians filled it with new meaning from the love God showed in Christ. Read the chapter with Jesus’ name in place of “love” and it describes him; read it with your own name and it shows how far you fall short.

First Paul shows that love is essential. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, even giving away everything or sacrificing one’s body, are worth nothing without love. Then he describes love in action, mostly by what it does not do, and almost every phrase corrects something in Corinth: envy, boasting, arrogance, rudeness, self-seeking. Finally he shows that love lasts. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge are partial and temporary, suited to the present age, like a child’s speech or a dim reflection in a bronze mirror. When the complete arrives, at Christ’s return, they will give way to seeing God face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Paul could speak every human language and even the language of angels, but had no love, he would be no more than a noisy gong or a clashing cymbal. If he had the gift of prophecy and understood every mystery and all knowledge, and had faith enough to move mountains, but had no love, he would be nothing. If he gave away everything he owned and handed over his body to hardship, but had no love, he would gain nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Aquinas, following Augustine, called love (caritas) the form of all virtues — the quality without which no virtue is genuinely virtuous. Paul’s three strophes make the same point: spiritual gifts without love are not merely incomplete but negated. Reformed theology has grounded this in the law of love (Matt 22:37–40): the whole law is fulfilled in love, and therefore the whole Christian life, including the exercise of spiritual gifts, finds its telos and criterion in love. The gift that is not exercised in love has been severed from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-speaker who exercised his gift in a public meeting, leaving the congregation uninstructed and himself privately edified, was exhibiting Paul’s noisy gong in practice. The spiritual trophy was real; the love was absent; the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than the people he is preaching to, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he is arguing with, the worship leader who loves the experience he generates more than the congregation he is leading — all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without love, the most spectacular gifts of speech, knowledge and faith amount to nothing.

Tongues of angels. Paul starts with the Corinthians’ favourite gift. Some Jewish writings imagined angels speaking a heavenly language; some Corinthians may have thought their tongues were angelic speech. Paul says even that, without love, is noise.

Gong and cymbal. Bronze instruments used in pagan worship, especially in the cults of Cybele and Dionysus, to create a frenzy. Corinth was famous for its bronze. Loud, impressive, empty.

Prophecy, mysteries, knowledge, faith. The most valued gifts. Faith to move mountains echoes Jesus’ words about “faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Matthew 17:20).

I am nothing. Not “my gift is nothing” but “I am nothing”. A gifted person without love has no spiritual worth.

On a Tuesday. A brilliant preacher who belittles his staff, a skilled worship leader who is jealous of others: they are clanging cymbals. Gifts are no substitute for love.
verseByVerse.note: Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without love, even total sacrifice gains nothing.

Give away all. Literally “feed out in morsels”, giving away possessions bit by bit to the hungry. Generosity without love may be for show: “when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do” (Matthew 6:2).

Burned, or boast? A significant textual variant.

“That I may be burned” (kauthēsomai; KJV, ESV text): perhaps martyrdom, or slavery, since slaves were sometimes branded. An Indian holy man had famously burned himself to death in Athens in Augustus’s time, and his tomb there was a tourist attraction.

“That I may boast” (kauchēsomai; ESV footnote; the earliest papyrus and the major early manuscripts): handing over the body to suffering in order to have grounds for boasting.

Verdict: “that I may boast” is better attested in the earliest manuscripts and fits the theme of boasting in this letter; many modern translations prefer it. The point is the same: even the greatest sacrifice, done without love, gains nothing.

On a Tuesday. Ask why you give or serve. For recognition, or out of love?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body [to death] that I may boast.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love is patient and kind. It is not envious, boastful or proud. It does not behave disgracefully, does not seek its own advantage, is not easily provoked, and keeps no record of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing but is glad when truth wins. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes and always perseveres.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Christological Description

The point deserves full weight: replace “love” in vv. 4–7 with “Jesus Christ” and the sentences remain true. Christ is patient — he waited thirty years before beginning his public ministry; he bore with his disciples for three years; he endured the cross. Christ is kind — he touched lepers, welcomed children, ate with sinners. Christ does not insist on his own way — “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Christ does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth. Christ bears all things, believes all things (his faith was perfect toward the Father), hopes all things (the joy set before him, Heb 12:2), endures all things (the cross). Love is not primarily a commandment to be obeyed but a Person to be united with — and as Christ is formed in us (Gal 4:19), his character becomes our character.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth. Every community that reads 1 Corinthians 13 should see itself in it — not as an aspiration but as a diagnostic. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? The catalogue of love’s character is simultaneously a catalogue of the community’s failures. Now: The most powerful apologetic for Christianity in the twenty-first century is not a philosophical argument but a community that actually loves this way — that bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The watching world knows what love looks like; it is waiting to see if the church produces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is patient and kind, and free of envy, boasting and pride.

Patient. Makrothymei: long-tempered, slow to anger, especially towards people who are difficult. God’s own character (Exodus 34:6).

Kind. Actively good to others.

Does not envy. The Corinthians were jealous of each other’s gifts and leaders (3:3).

Does not boast. Perpereuetai: does not brag, show off, sing its own praises.

Not arrogant. Physioutai: not puffed up, the word Paul has used against them repeatedly (4:6, 18; 5:2; 8:1).

Jesus in this verse. Jesus was patient with slow disciples, kind to outcasts, never envious, never boastful: “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Love is not first a feeling but a way of acting, and its model is Christ.

On a Tuesday. Put your own name in place of “love”: “[Name] is patient, [Name] is kind…”. Where does it stop being true?

parallels.desc: love covers all offences

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is not rude, selfish, irritable or resentful.

Not rude. Does not behave disgracefully or indecently, as at their Lord’s Supper (11:21–22) or in their worship (11:4–5).

Not insisting on its own way. Does not seek its own advantage (10:24, 33).

Not irritable. Not touchy, easily provoked.

Not resentful. Literally “does not reckon the evil”: an accounting word. Love does not keep a ledger of wrongs to bring up later. “Love covers all offenses” (Proverbs 10:12).

On a Tuesday. Is there someone whose past wrongs you keep bringing up? Tear up the ledger.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love takes no pleasure in wrong but rejoices in the truth.

Not rejoicing at wrong. Not enjoying gossip about others’ failures, not pleased when a rival falls, not proud of tolerating sin (5:2).

Rejoices with the truth. Love and truth go together. Love is not soft on sin; it is glad when truth and right prevail.

What it does not mean. Love is not the same as tolerance of everything. Biblical love tells the truth and wants what is right for the other person.

On a Tuesday. When you hear bad news about someone you dislike, notice your reaction. Love grieves.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love bears, believes, hopes and endures all things.

Bears all things. Stegei: covers, as a roof covers a house, or endures. Love protects others, covering their faults rather than exposing them: “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

Believes all things. Not gullibility, but readiness to think the best of others, to give the benefit of the doubt.

Hopes all things. Love does not give up on people.

Endures all things. Hypomenei: holds out under pressure. Love keeps going.

What it does not mean. Not that love puts up with abuse indefinitely or believes lies. Love protects the vulnerable and rejoices with the truth (v. 6).

On a Tuesday. A wife caring for a husband with dementia, a parent waiting for a prodigal: these are love that bears, hopes and endures.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love never fails. Prophecies will come to an end, tongues will stop, and knowledge will pass away, because our knowledge and our prophecy are only partial, and when completeness comes, the partial will be done away with. When Paul was a child he talked, thought and reasoned like a child, but when he became a man he put childish ways behind him. At present we see only a blurred reflection in a mirror, but then we shall see face to face. Now Paul knows in part; then he will know fully, just as he is fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of them is love.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatology of the Gifts and the Permanence of Love

Paul’s teaching that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away is often taken as the foundation of the cessationist argument — the gifts being provisional for an age of incomplete revelation and superseded when the perfect comes. Whether the perfect means the completion of the New Testament canon, the maturity of the church, or the return of Christ has been debated for centuries; but Paul defines his own terms in verse 12, where then is when we see face to face and know fully even as I have been fully known. Since no one began to see God face to face when the canon closed, this passage by itself does not settle the question, and the stronger arguments for cessation are made from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4 rather than from here. Those arguments are the stronger.

What the passage does settle is the structure: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever. A church that pours its energy into the spectacular while neglecting love has it exactly backwards, clinging to the provisional and letting go of the permanent — and that is true of every party to the argument, whichever side it takes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian community that prized tongues above all else was, on Paul’s analysis, investing heavily in something that would not survive the transition to the coming age, while neglecting the one quality that would. Now: The church that is rich in programmes, gifts, and spiritual activity but thin in genuine love has the Corinthian problem in contemporary dress. Every spiritual tradition — charismatic, Reformed, liturgical — can produce communities that are impressively gifted and loveless. Paul’s word is the same to all of them: love never ends; everything else is provisional.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never ends, but the gifts of prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away.

Love never ends. Love is eternal, because God is love (1 John 4:8).

Gifts are temporary. The very gifts the Corinthians prized belong to this age only.

Knowledge. Not all knowledge, but the gift of knowledge, partial insight into God’s truth.

On a Tuesday. Invest in what lasts. Spiritual gifts are tools; love is the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our knowledge now is partial, and will give way when the complete comes.

In part. All our knowledge of God in this life is partial, even with the gifts.

What is “the perfect”? To teleion: the complete, the finished.

The completed New Testament: some cessationists argue that when Scripture was complete, the partial gifts ceased.

The mature church.

The return of Christ and the final state, when we see face to face (v. 12).

Verdict: the return of Christ. Only then will we see “face to face” and know as we are known. This was Calvin’s view and is held by most cessationists today, such as Richard Gaffin, as well as continuationists. So this verse does not itself prove that the gifts have ceased; the cessationist case rests on other passages, such as Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4. Honesty about this matters.

On a Tuesday. Even the best Bible teacher knows only in part. Hold your theology humbly.
verseByVerse.note: “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things when Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The present gifts belong to the church’s childhood, compared with the maturity to come.

Childhood and adulthood. Our present life, even with spiritual gifts, is like childhood compared with the life to come. The gifts are suited to this stage.

A gentle rebuke. The Corinthians, proud of their gifts, were behaving like children (3:1; 14:20).

On a Tuesday. Grow up in love. Maturity is measured by love, not by experiences.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we see dimly, but then we shall see face to face and know fully, as we are known.

A mirror dimly. Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, and Corinth was famous for its bronze work. They gave a real but blurred image. Literally “in a riddle” (en ainigmati), echoing God’s words about Moses: “With him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8).

Face to face. Seeing God directly, the “beatific vision” as the church has called it. “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Fully known. God already knows us completely (8:3). One day we will know him as fully as a creature can.

For worship. Thank God that one day you will see him face to face. Let that hope steady you today.
verseByVerse.note: Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect reflection; Corinth was famous for its bronze work. The ESV notes that “dimly” is literally “in a riddle.”

parallels.desc: with him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles

verseByVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love.

Faith, hope and love. Paul’s triad (1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8; Colossians 1:4–5). Faith trusts God, hope looks forward to his promises, love gives itself to God and others.

Abide. Unlike the gifts, these remain. Some say faith and hope will end when we see and possess what we hoped for (Romans 8:24). Others say they continue in heaven in a new form, as trust and expectation. Either way, love is the greatest because it alone will go on unchanged, and because God himself is love.

The greatest. Love is greater than faith, which saves us; than hope, which steadies us; and than every gift.

For worship. “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Thank him for loving you first, and ask him to love others through you this week.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.<sup>2</sup>And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.<sup>3</sup>If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.<sup>4</sup>Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant<sup>5</sup>or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;<sup>6</sup>it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.<sup>7</sup>Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.<sup>8</sup>Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.<sup>9</sup>For we know in part and we prophesy in part,<sup>10</sup>but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.<sup>11</sup>When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.<sup>12</sup>For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Having shown that love is the way all gifts must be used, Paul applies it to the Corinthians’ worship, which had become noisy and confusing as many people spoke in tongues at once. His test is simple: what builds up the church? Tongues spoken without interpretation build up only the speaker, because no one else understands; prophecy, spoken in ordinary language, strengthens, encourages and comforts everyone. Like a flute that plays no recognisable tune, or a bugle with an uncertain call, unintelligible speech helps nobody, and a visitor cannot even say “Amen” to a prayer he does not understand. Paul himself speaks in tongues more than all of them, but in church he would rather say five words people can understand than ten thousand in a tongue.

He quotes Isaiah, where foreign speech was a sign of God’s judgement on unbelieving Israel, and warns that a visitor who walks into a room full of tongues will think they are mad, whereas prophecy may expose his heart and bring him to worship God. Then he gives practical rules. Each person may contribute, a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation, but everything must build others up. Only two or three should speak in tongues, in turn, with interpretation; two or three prophets should speak and the others weigh what they say. God is a God of peace, not disorder. Women should keep silent in this setting, apparently in the weighing of prophecies. Paul’s instructions are the Lord’s command, and everything should be done decently and in order.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to make love their aim, and to desire spiritual gifts eagerly, especially prophecy. Someone who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, not to people, because no one understands; he utters mysteries by the Spirit. But someone who prophesies speaks to people, building them up, encouraging and comforting them. The tongue-speaker edifies himself, but the prophet edifies the church. Paul would like every one of them to speak in tongues, but he would rather they prophesied. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Intelligibility as a Prerequisite for Edification

Paul’s governing principle for corporate worship — intelligibility — has deep theological roots. The God who speaks is a God who communicates; the Word became flesh precisely to be heard and understood. Worship that renders the word of God inaccessible to the gathered community is, at a structural level, working against the grain of the incarnation. The Reformers’ insistence on vernacular worship (against the Latin Mass) was an application of precisely this principle: if the people cannot understand what is being said and done, they cannot be edified.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues in corporate worship was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the faction fights: tongues was the impressive gift, the spectacular performance. Paul’s preference for prophecy is a preference for the communal over the spectacular, the edifying over the impressive. Now: The principle of intelligibility has applications beyond tongues: jargon-laden sermons, inaccessible liturgy, and culturally opaque worship practices all fail the same criterion. Does the person who attends understand what is happening? Are they being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue love, and desire gifts that serve others, especially prophecy rather than uninterpreted tongues.

Pursue love. The link with chapter 13. Love chooses the gifts that help others.

Especially prophecy. Because it is understood by all.

Speaks to God. Tongues are directed to God in prayer or praise (vv. 2, 14–16), not as a message to the church, unless interpreted.

Mysteries. Things hidden from the hearers, because they cannot understand the language.

On a Tuesday. In any gathering, prefer what everyone can understand. Avoid jargon that leaves visitors outside.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophecy speaks to people for their building up, encouragement and comfort.

What was New Testament prophecy?

Some continuationists (Wayne Grudem) see it as a report of something God brings to mind, carrying less authority than Scripture and able to contain errors, which is why it must be weighed (v. 29).

Cessationists see it as revelation from God with real authority, part of the foundation laid by apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), which ceased when the New Testament was complete.

Many Puritans called preaching “prophesying” (William Perkins wrote The Art of Prophesying, a manual on preaching), applying Paul’s principles to the exposition of Scripture.

Verdict: New Testament prophecy was a gift of revelation (v. 30) belonging to the founding of the church. Today its function of strengthening, encouraging and comforting the church through God’s word is carried on by the faithful preaching and teaching of Scripture. But Christians on all sides agree with Paul’s main point: speech that builds others up is to be preferred to speech no one understands.

Three purposes. Upbuilding (strengthening faith), encouragement (urging on), consolation (comforting the sad).

On a Tuesday. Measure any sermon, Bible study or word of advice by these three. Did it build up, encourage and comfort?

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tongues build up the speaker, but prophecy builds up the church.

Builds up himself. Not a selfish thing in itself; private prayer builds up the believer. But church gatherings are for others.

I want you all to speak in tongues. Paul does not despise tongues (v. 39). But he has already said not all will (12:30).

Greater. More useful, more loving, because it serves the church.

Private tongues today? Many charismatic Christians use tongues as a private prayer language. Cessationists believe the genuine gift has ceased and that modern tongues are a learned human ability. Verdict: held charitably; but whatever one’s view, Paul’s rule is clear: in public worship, intelligibility is required.

On a Tuesday. When choosing how to serve, choose what helps others most, not what makes you feel most spiritual.

parallels.desc: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks what good it would do them if he came speaking in tongues and brought no revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching. Even lifeless instruments, a flute or a harp, must play distinct notes to be recognised, and if a trumpet sounds an unclear call, who will prepare for battle? It is the same with them: unintelligible speech is talking into the air. There are many languages in the world, all meaningful, but if Paul does not understand a language he and the speaker are foreigners to each other. Since they are eager for spiritual gifts, they should seek to excel in those that build up the church. So anyone who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret. If Paul prays in a tongue, his spirit prays but his mind is unproductive. So he will pray and sing both with his spirit and with his mind. Otherwise, how can an outsider say “Amen” to his thanksgiving if he does not know what is being said? He may give thanks well, but the other person is not built up. Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them, but in church he would rather speak five words that teach others than ten thousand in a tongue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Corporate Criterion and the Nature of Worship

Paul’s insistence on intelligibility in corporate worship reflects a deep theological conviction about the nature of Christian assembly: it is not a private spiritual experience shared simultaneously by many individuals but a genuinely corporate event in which the whole body is built up together. Worship is not merely my encounter with God in the presence of other people; it is our encounter with God as a body. This corporate dimension requires intelligibility: I cannot say “Amen” to what I cannot understand, and a community of “Amens” is the sign that the body is genuinely worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-enthusiasts were essentially importing an individual spiritual practice into the corporate meeting without consideration for the community’s ability to participate. Paul’s five-to-ten-thousand ratio is not a rule to be calculated but a principle to be embodied: always ask, in corporate worship, whether what is done can be received and responded to by the whole community. Now: The principle applies to any element of worship that prioritises the experience of some over the edification of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speech that others cannot understand is no help to them.

Four kinds of intelligible speech. Revelation and prophecy, knowledge and teaching. Paul’s own ministry depended on these, not on tongues.

On a Tuesday. Ask what a visitor would learn about God from your church’s service.

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even instruments must give distinct sounds to be understood.

The flute and lyre. The aulos (a double reed pipe) and the kithara (lyre), common at banquets, weddings and funerals. Random notes make no tune.

The trumpet. In the army, trumpet calls signalled advance, retreat or assembly. An unclear call would be disastrous.

On a Tuesday. Preachers, teachers and parents: give a clear sound. Vague or confusing teaching leaves people unprepared.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet sounded signals to soldiers in battle.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unintelligible speech is just noise to the hearer.

Foreigner. Barbaros: the Greek word for anyone who did not speak Greek, supposedly because their speech sounded like “bar-bar” to Greek ears. From it comes our “barbarian”.

Languages. This suggests tongues were understood as languages, if unknown to the hearers.

On a Tuesday. In a multilingual church, take care that worship is understood. Provide translation where you can.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since they are eager for gifts, they should excel in those that build up the church.

Eager for manifestations. Literally “zealous for spirits”. Paul redirects their zeal.

On a Tuesday. Desire to be useful in your church more than to be impressive.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tongues should be interpreted, and worship must engage the mind as well as the spirit.

Pray to interpret. The aim is understanding.

Spirit and mind. Paul wants both. Christian worship engages the whole person, emotions and intellect together. Neither cold rationalism nor mindless ecstasy.

On a Tuesday. When you sing in church, think about the words. When you pray, mean what you say.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An outsider cannot say amen to what he cannot understand.

Amen. From the synagogue, where the people responded “Amen” to prayers (Nehemiah 8:6). The congregation joins the prayer by saying “so be it”.

The outsider. Idiōtēs: an uninstructed person, perhaps a visitor or enquirer. Worship should be accessible to them.

On a Tuesday. Say “Amen” aloud in church when you agree with a prayer. It is your part in it.
verseByVerse.note: “Amen” (“so be it”) was the congregation’s response to prayer and thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul would rather speak five words with his mind than ten thousand in a tongue.

More than all of you. Paul is not against tongues because he lacks the gift.

Five words. A deliberate contrast: five against ten thousand (a myriad, the largest Greek number word). Five understandable words are worth more.

On a Tuesday. A short, clear explanation of the gospel to a friend is worth more than a long, impressive speech they do not understand.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to stop thinking like children; they should be infants in evil but adults in their thinking. Scripture says that God would speak to his people through people of strange tongues and foreign lips, and even then they would not listen. So tongues are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers, while prophecy is for believers, not unbelievers. If the whole church meets and everyone speaks in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers come in, they will say the believers are out of their minds. But if everyone prophesies and an unbeliever or outsider comes in, he will be convicted and judged by all, the secrets of his heart will be laid bare, and he will fall down and worship God, declaring that God is really among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who might walk in to the church meeting is a significant ecclesiological statement: corporate worship is not only for the already-converted. The community that worships in such a way that the outsider can be addressed, convicted, and drawn to worship is doing something the tongues-heavy meeting cannot do. This does not make evangelism the primary purpose of corporate worship — the primary purpose is the glorification of God — but it recognises that intelligible worship of the living God is inherently missionary in its effect.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meetings were apparently chaotic — multiple tongues-speakers simultaneously, no interpretation, no order. Paul’s Isaiah citation turns their spiritual pride upside down: the tongues without interpretation is a sign associated with divine judgment, not divine favour. Now: The church that makes its corporate worship impenetrable to the outsider — whether through uninterpreted ecstatic experience, impenetrable theological jargon, or cultural inscrutability — is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be the thing that disturbs, not the incomprehensibility of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must be mature in thinking; tongues are a sign of judgment for unbelievers.

Children. The Corinthians were fascinated by tongues like children with a new toy. Jesus did call us to become like children (Matthew 18:3), in humility and trust, not in immaturity of thought.

Isaiah 28:11. “By people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people.” In Isaiah, Jerusalem’s leaders mocked the prophet’s message as baby-talk. God replied that since they would not listen to him in plain Hebrew, he would speak to them through the foreign language of the Assyrian invaders, a sign of judgement, as Moses had warned (Deuteronomy 28:49, “a nation whose language you do not understand”).

A sign for unbelievers. Tongues without interpretation do not convert unbelievers; they confirm them in their unbelief. Some cessationists (such as O. Palmer Robertson) argue that tongues were a sign of judgement on unbelieving Israel, marking the shift of God’s work to the nations, and so ceased once that transition was complete. Verdict: a strong argument, consistent with Acts, though not the only way to read the verse.

Law. Here “the Law” means the Old Testament as a whole.

On a Tuesday. Think like a grown-up about spiritual experiences: test them by Scripture and by their fruit.
verseByVerse.note: “The Law” here means the Scriptures. In Isaiah, foreign speech — the Assyrian invaders — was a sign of judgment on those who refused to listen.

parallels.desc: by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Uncontrolled tongues make outsiders think the church is mad.

Out of your minds. Mainesthe: raving, like the frenzied worshippers of Dionysus. The visitor would think the church was just another ecstatic cult.

Convicted. Prophecy, in understandable words, reaches the conscience.

Evangelism in worship. Paul expects unbelievers to visit church services. Worship should be clear enough to reach them.

On a Tuesday. Invite a non-Christian friend to church. Pray that the word preached would reach their heart.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clear prophetic speech exposes the heart and leads outsiders to worship God.

Secrets disclosed. The visitor feels that the message speaks directly to his hidden life, as the Samaritan woman said of Jesus, “He told me all that I ever did” (John 4:39).

God is really among you. Echoing Isaiah 45:14, where the nations confess to Israel, “Surely God is in you, and there is no other.” The prophecy of the Gentiles’ conversion is fulfilled in the church.

For worship. Pray for this in your church: that visitors will meet God, not just a good meeting.

parallels.desc: God is with you only
we have heard that God is with you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When they meet, each person may bring a hymn, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation, but everything must be done to build up the church. If anyone speaks in a tongue, there should be two, or at most three, one at a time, and someone must interpret; without an interpreter the speaker should keep quiet in church and speak to himself and to God. Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh what is said. If a revelation comes to someone else who is sitting there, the first speaker should stop. They can all prophesy in turn, so that everyone learns and is encouraged. The spirits of prophets are under the prophets’ control, because God is not a God of disorder but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints, women are to keep silent in the assemblies; they are not allowed to speak but should be in submission, as the law also says. If they want to learn something, they should ask their husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. Did the word of God begin with the Corinthians, or are they the only people it has reached? Anyone who thinks he is a prophet or spiritual should acknowledge that what Paul writes is the Lord’s command. Anyone who ignores this will himself be ignored. So they should eagerly desire to prophesy and not forbid speaking in tongues, but everything should be done in a fitting and orderly way.
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

The theological ground for orderly worship — “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” — is a direct application of the doctrine of God to liturgical practice. The triune God is the most perfectly ordered being there is: the three persons in eternal, loving, ordered communion. Worship that is chaotic and disorderly is, at a deep level, a misrepresentation of the God being worshipped. Conversely, worship that is ordered, intelligible, and participatory is an enacted icon of the divine order. The Reformers understood this: the liturgical reforms of Geneva and Zurich were not mere preference but a theological conviction that worship should reflect the character of the God it addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meeting was apparently chaotic: multiple simultaneous tongues, no weighing of prophecies, a general air of competitive spiritual display. Paul’s practical rules — two or three, in turn, with evaluation — are not bureaucratic restrictions but pastoral wisdom about how a community can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: “Decently and in order” is the guiding principle for every aspect of church life, from Sunday worship to congregational meetings to pastoral care. Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the condition in which the Spirit’s gifts can be received and used by the whole community.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in worship must be done for building up.

Each one. Corinthian worship was participatory: many contributed. Not a spectator event.

Five contributions. A hymn (perhaps a psalm), a lesson (teaching), a revelation (prophecy), a tongue, an interpretation.

For building up. The governing rule of all worship.

How should worship be ordered today? Reformed churches have generally held the “regulative principle”: worship should include only what God commands in Scripture (reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments). Other traditions hold that whatever Scripture does not forbid is allowed. Verdict: the regulative principle, applied with wisdom. This chapter shows that apostolic worship was word-centred, orderly and congregational: Christ’s word dwelling richly as believers teach and sing (Colossians 3:16).

On a Tuesday. Come to church to give, not only to receive: sing heartily, pray, encourage someone.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tongues must be limited, in turn, and interpreted, or else kept silent.

Limits. Two or three, one at a time, interpreted. Not a crowd all at once.

Self-control. Tongues could be held back. The speaker was not in an uncontrollable trance.

On a Tuesday. If your church allows tongues, it should keep Paul’s rules.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets should speak in turn, and others weigh what is said.

Weigh. Diakrinetōsan: evaluate, discern. Prophecy was tested by the church. “Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). In the Old Testament, a prophet whose words failed was false (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Revelation. Prophecy came by revelation.

All may learn. The goal again: teaching and encouragement.

On a Tuesday. Weigh what you hear preached against Scripture, like the Bereans, who examined “the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11).

parallels.desc: test everything

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets can control themselves, for God is a God of peace, not disorder.

Under control. Unlike pagan prophets, who claimed to be overpowered by the god, Christian prophets could control themselves. The Spirit does not override the person.

A God of peace. Chaos in worship misrepresents God.

As in all the churches. Many translations attach this phrase to verse 34 instead. Either way, Paul appeals to the practice of the wider church.

On a Tuesday. If someone claims the Spirit made them do something disorderly or harmful, remember this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women should not take part in the authoritative weighing of prophecy in the assembly.

A hard verse. Paul has already said women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). So he cannot mean total silence. What then?

Christians hold four main views.

Not Paul’s words: some scholars (notably Gordon Fee) argue these verses were added later, because in some Western manuscripts they appear after verse 40 rather than here.

Disruptive questions: women, often less educated, were interrupting with questions, and should ask at home.

Weighing prophecies: women should not take part in the authoritative evaluation of prophecy (v. 29), which would mean judging the men who prophesied (D. A. Carson, Wayne Grudem).

Total silence: some groups have taken it literally, forbidding women to speak at all in services.

Verdict: the third, perhaps with something of the second. The verses are in every manuscript (they are only moved in a few), so they are genuine Scripture. The context is the weighing of prophecy; the appeal to submission and to the law (probably the creation order of Genesis 2, as in 11:8–9 and 1 Timothy 2:12–13) fits a ban on authoritative judging and teaching of men, not on speaking at all.

A textual note. A few Western manuscripts place verses 34–35 after verse 40. The best explanation is that a scribe moved them to keep the discussion of prophecy unbroken. No manuscript omits them.

On a Tuesday. Whatever your church’s practice, honour the women who serve, pray, sing, teach children and other women, and give wise counsel. Paul assumed women would pray and prophesy.
verseByVerse.note: Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Interpreters differ on what speaking is forbidden here; many take it as the public judging of prophecies just mentioned (v. 29).

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Corinthians are not the source or sole possessors of God’s word.

Corinthian pride. They acted as if they could make their own rules, ignoring the practice of the other churches.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of churches or movements that claim to have discovered truth no one else has seen.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
True spiritual people will recognise Paul’s words as the Lord’s command.

The Lord’s command. Paul claims that his words carry Christ’s authority. A true prophet will recognise apostolic authority. This is the basis of the New Testament canon: the apostles’ writings are the Lord’s word.

Not recognised. Either “let him be ignored” by the church, or “he is not recognised” by God.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ between “he is not recognised” (passive statement) and “let him be ignorant” (KJV, a command). The first is better attested.

On a Tuesday. If any spiritual experience or prophecy contradicts the plain teaching of Scripture, reject it. Scripture has the final word.

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Desire to prophesy, do not forbid tongues, but do all things decently and in order.

Do not forbid tongues. Paul did not ban tongues in Corinth.

And today? Cessationists believe the gift of tongues ceased with the apostolic age, so that this instruction applied to the churches while the gift existed. Continuationists believe this verse forbids churches to ban tongues today. Verdict: Paul’s command assumes the gift was present; whether it is present now must be settled from the wider teaching of Scripture. Christians on both sides should keep Paul’s principles of love, intelligibility and order, and treat each other with charity.

Decently and in order. The last word on worship. Beauty, reverence and order, not confusion.

For worship. Pray that your church’s worship will build up believers and reach visitors, for the glory of the God of peace.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.<sup>6</sup>Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?<sup>7</sup>If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played?<sup>8</sup>And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?<sup>9</sup>So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.<sup>10</sup>There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning,<sup>11</sup>but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.<sup>12</sup>So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.<sup>14</sup>For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.<sup>16</sup>Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?<sup>17</sup>For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.<sup>18</sup>I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.<sup>20</sup>Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.<sup>21</sup>In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”<sup>22</sup>Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.<sup>23</sup>If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?<sup>24</sup>But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,<sup>25</sup>the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.<sup>26</sup>What then, brothers?
